planting.note: Sow fresh seed on the soil surface in fall and allow natural winter cold to break dormancy, or set out nursery plugs beneath sandstone overhangs and shaded bluff faces in humus-rich, gravelly, well-drained soil.

directions: French's shooting star is a regional specialist of shaded sandstone bluffs and canyon walls across the lower Midwest, rooting into thin, mossy soil pockets under overhanging rock rather than open forest floor like most of its relatives. Magenta-pink, reflexed petals surround a dark, beak-like cluster of stamens on nodding flowers held above a low rosette of spoon-shaped leaves in mid-spring. Like other shooting stars it is a true spring ephemeral, with foliage yellowing and vanishing completely by early summer once seed has set. Because it is uncommon and slow to establish, plant only nursery-propagated stock and avoid disturbing the shallow, fibrous root system once sited.

common_name: White Shooting Star (Pacific Northwest Streamside Native)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall and let winter cold stratify it naturally, or plant nursery divisions into a consistently moist, cool, rocky site beside a streambank or shaded seep in humus-rich soil.

directions: Unlike most shooting stars, this Pacific Northwest native favors shaded streambanks, mossy rock crevices, and seepage areas in coniferous forest rather than drier open woods, and its toothed leaf margins, reflected in the species name, distinguish it from similar relatives. Pure white, strongly reflexed flowers with a dark anther tube nod atop leafless stalks in late spring, rising just above a basal rosette of glossy leaves. It is a spring ephemeral that goes dormant by midsummer as the streamside vegetation fills in around it. Keep soil reliably moist through the growing season, since this species is markedly less drought-tolerant than its drier-habitat relatives.

planting.note: Sow seed in fall to take advantage of winter rains, or set out nursery plugs into fast-draining, humus-rich soil at the edge of oak woodland or beneath open shrubs; this California native germinates and grows through the cool, wet winter months.

directions: One of the earliest shooting stars to bloom, Padre's shooting star lights up grassy slopes and open oak woodland margins across coastal and interior California as early as midwinter, with deep magenta-pink petals swept back from a dark central cone. It grows through the rainy season on winter moisture, flowering and setting seed before summer drought sets in, then dies back completely to its underground corm for the dry months. In cultivation it wants the same Mediterranean rhythm: damp, humus-rich soil and light shade from fall through spring, followed by a dry summer rest with little to no irrigation. It combines well with other California woodland natives that share this winter-wet, summer-dry cycle.

common_name: Sierra Shooting Star (Tall Mountain Shooting Star)

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring into consistently wet, humus-rich soil near a pond edge, seep, or partially shaded streamside bed that mimics its native mountain meadow habitat.

directions: The largest of the western shooting stars, this species forms substantial colonies in wet subalpine and montane meadows, streambanks, and seeps across the Sierra Nevada, Cascades, and northern Rockies, often blooming in masses just after snowmelt. Each tall, leafless stalk carries several deep magenta flowers with swept-back petals and a dark, pointed beak of fused anthers, held well above the basal foliage. In lowland gardens it appreciates a cooler, consistently damp site with afternoon shade, since it naturally grows where snowmelt keeps roots wet through the bloom period. Foliage yellows and disappears by late summer once soil dries, in keeping with its ephemeral habit.

planting.note: Plant dormant corms or divisions in fall or very early spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in a partially shaded bed or meadow planting; this selection is propagated by division to preserve its deeper flower color.

directions: This selection of the widespread prairie shooting star was chosen for flowers in a notably deeper wine-red to magenta shade than the straight species' usual pink-lavender, with the same swept-back petals and dark central beak that give the whole genus its common name. It blooms in mid-spring in moist meadows, streambanks, and open woodland edges across much of western and central North America, then goes summer-dormant as its habitat dries out. In the garden it performs best with reliable spring moisture and light shade, tapering off on water once the foliage begins to yellow. Established clumps slowly multiply by offsets and can be divided after flowering while still visible.

common_name: Minnesota Dwarf Trout Lily (Federally Threatened Endemic)

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated bulblets in fall, 3-4 inches deep, into deep, moist, humus-rich floodplain-forest soil in full shade; never collect from the wild, as this species is federally listed as threatened and restricted to a small area of southeastern Minnesota.

directions: This diminutive trout lily is a true conservation rarity, found naturally only along a handful of maple-basswood floodplain forests in a few southeastern Minnesota counties, where it is federally protected as a threatened species. Its species name, roughly meaning 'to propel forward,' refers to its unusual habit of budding off small daughter bulbs on thread-like stolons, which is how most colonies spread since it rarely sets viable seed. Mottled leaves and small white to pale pink nodding flowers emerge in earliest spring and vanish by early summer, exactly like its more common trout lily relatives, but at a notably smaller scale throughout. Because wild populations are fragile and legally protected, grow only nursery-propagated material and give it the same rich, consistently moist floodplain-type soil it depends on in the wild.

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall into deep, humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath oaks or mixed conifers and be patient, as seedlings take several years to reach blooming size; alternatively plant dormant bulbs or divisions in fall.

directions: A lesser-known fawn lily of the Sierra Nevada foothills, this species produces mottled, lance-shaped leaves and nodding, creamy white flowers with a yellow throat, often with multiple flower stalks rising from a single bulb, which gives it its species name. It blooms in late winter to early spring in open oak and pine woodland, taking advantage of seasonal moisture before summer drought arrives, then retreats underground for the rest of the year. As with other western fawn lilies, seed-grown bulbs are slow to reach blooming size, often taking four or more years, so division of established clumps is the faster route to a mature planting. Give it the same winter-wet, summer-dry cycle it experiences in the wild, with light shade and excellent drainage.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled shade; this selection is grown for its dark foliage color and increases readily by division.

directions: This foliage selection of the native wild geranium emerges with rich chocolate-bronze young leaves that mature to a deep bronze-green through the season, a striking contrast to the plain green foliage of the wild type. Loose clusters of soft lavender-pink, five-petaled flowers open above the foliage in mid-spring, drawing early native bees, and continue intermittently into early summer. Unlike the true spring ephemerals in this list, wild geranium keeps its handsome foliage mound through summer and into fall rather than going dormant, making it a useful long-season companion planted around earlier-vanishing ephemerals like trout lily or Dutchman's breeches. Divide congested clumps in spring or fall to maintain vigor and increase the planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled shade; this sterile double-flowered selection must be propagated by division rather than seed.

directions: This selection of the native wild geranium carries fully double, soft pink pompon-like flowers in place of the simple five-petaled blooms of the wild type, a sport that arose spontaneously and has been maintained in cultivation by division ever since. Because the flowers lack functional reproductive parts, the plant cannot set seed and channels its energy into an extended bloom period through mid-spring into early summer instead. Clumps of lobed, deep green foliage persist attractively through the growing season and take on reddish tones in fall, unlike the ephemeral species in this list that disappear by midsummer. Divide clumps every few years in spring or fall, since this is the only way to propagate and spread the selection.

planting.note: Plant rooted divisions or nursery plugs in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade; this creeping selection spreads by surface stolons to form a dense mat.

directions: This white-flowered selection of creeping phlox forms a low, semi-evergreen mat of rounded leaves that roots as it spreads by surface stolons, making it a useful living mulch around taller woodland ephemerals. Clusters of flat-faced, pure white flowers with a faint pale eye open in mid-spring just above the foliage, drawing early butterflies and bees to the shade garden. Because its foliage persists through summer and winter rather than going dormant, it helps cover the bare ground left behind when nearby spring ephemerals like trout lily or Virginia bluebells disappear for the season. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mat tidy and encourage dense new growth.
